blocks.text: languages through which authority, resistance, duty, and daily life are imagined.” \[CIATION: Matthew J. Walton argues that Theravada Buddhism has provided both raw materials and a conceptual framework for politics in Myanmar, helping people defend authority, contest authority, and imagine forms of democratic morality. Jayde Lin Roberts, writing on Mandalay, shows how neighborhood life coheres around dhamma halls and moral relations that cross official ward boundaries; municipal authority may be inconsistent, but moral authority remains powerfully social. In the nineteenth century, during King Mindon’s reign in Mandalay, political instability and religious merit-making were not opposites: they were intertwined. The city of Buddhism was also a city of strategy. To say that Myanmar is spiritual, then, is true only if one also says that spirituality there has always lived close to politics, sometimes as conscience, sometimes as legitimacy, sometimes—dangerously—as ethnoreligious exclusion.\]
